transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello. Thank you for seeing me. I, um, I wasn't entirely sure if I should make the appointment, to be perfectly honest. It's just that things have been... well, a bit chaotic lately. But what finally pushed me to pick up the phone and actually come in today is that my eating has just been completely all over the place. I mean, it's really starting to bother me. Some weeks, I'll make a whole dinner, you know, a nice meal, and I just sit there staring at it. I barely touch a thing. I just don't have the stomach for it, or the interest, or whatever you want to call it. But then, it's like a switch flips, and other nights—and this has been happening more often than I'd like to admit—I'll find myself standing in the middle of the kitchen at two in the morning, long after everyone else has gone to bed and the house is completely quiet, and I'm just eating. Crackers, cookies, whatever sweets I can find in the pantry. I just stand there in the dark eating, and I don't even really feel hungry when I do it, but I can't seem to stop myself. It's just so frustrating because I used to be fairly regular with my meals, and now I just don't know what my body wants from one day to the next.
Do you usually feel guilty after these late-night eating episodes?

Oh, guilty... yes, absolutely. But to be perfectly honest with you, it’s not just the cookies or the crackers that make me feel that way. It’s... well, it's everything. The guilt is just so heavy lately, like a physical weight sitting right on my chest. I mean, I can spend hours—literally hours, just sitting there in the living room while the sun goes down—replaying these incredibly small, almost insignificant things in my head. 

Like, just the other week, I bought this expensive tube of pigment. I dabble in art, you know, just some painting here and there when I can focus, and I thought, 'Oh, I'll treat myself, it's just one color.' But the second I paid for it, I just spiraled. I spent the rest of the day and half the night agonizing over it, thinking about how selfish I am, how I shouldn't have spent that money when we have other bills. Or, another example, if I just snap at my spouse—just a tiny, passing irritable comment because I'm feeling stressed out—I will replay that five-second interaction over and over and over again. I analyze my tone of voice, the look on his face, the silence in the room afterward... and it just builds up in my head until I genuinely feel like I’ve ruined the whole household because of it. Like I'm this horrible, destructive force just ruining my family's peace over a tube of paint or a sharp word. 

So, yes, standing in the pantry eating makes me feel guilty, but it's really just a drop in the bucket compared to how I beat myself up over every little thing I do or say. It's just exhausting, honestly, feeling like every tiny misstep is a catastrophe.
Do you find that you eat more or less when you're feeling overwhelmed or stressed?

Well, that's exactly the thing, isn't it? It's so hard to pin down because it really just depends on the week, or even the day. Like I was saying before, that's really what finally pushed me to make this appointment and actually come in to see you. My eating has just been completely all over the place, and it's so tied to how overwhelmed I'm feeling. 

Sometimes, when the stress is just sitting there, heavy and suffocating, I'll make dinner—like a whole, proper dinner, maybe a roast or something that takes a lot of effort—and I'll sit down at the table and I just can't do it. I barely touch a thing. I just push the food around on my plate, and the thought of chewing and swallowing just feels like climbing a mountain. I have zero appetite. 

But then, when the stress shifts, or maybe when I'm just so exhausted from worrying all day, it goes the complete opposite direction. That's when I have those nights I mentioned, where I'm just standing in the kitchen at two in the morning. Everyone else is asleep, the house is totally dark, and I'm just eating whatever I can get my hands on. Crackers, sweets, cookies... just mindlessly eating. And it's not even about being hungry, it's just this compulsion, I guess? So it's both. I eat way less sometimes, and way, way more other times, and I just can't seem to find any sort of middle ground anymore.
Do you think you eat at those late-night times as a way to try and feel better when you're stressed or overwhelmed?

Well, I suppose that might be part of it, trying to feel better, but honestly, it's just so confusing. I mean, I don't consciously think, 'Oh, I'm stressed, let me go eat a box of cookies.' It's more like a trance. But really, like I said earlier—and I know I'm repeating myself, but it's just so central to everything right now—what finally pushed me to pick up the phone and come in to see you is that my eating has just been completely all over the place. 

It's just so erratic. Some weeks, like I mentioned, I will make a lovely dinner, set the table, sit down, and I barely touch it. I just stare at the food and I can't bring myself to eat a single bite. And then, the flip side of that is standing in the kitchen at two in the morning, long after my husband is asleep, just eating crackers and sweets in the dark. It's not even about the taste at that point, it's just the action of it. So whether it's to feel better or just because I can't stop my brain from buzzing, the result is the same. I'm either starving myself by accident or eating everything in the pantry, and I just don't know how to stop the pendulum from swinging so wildly.
Do you ever feel like you've lost control during those late-night eating episodes?

Loss of control? Um, I don't... I don't know if I'd use the word "control," exactly. It's not like I'm possessed or something, or like my hands are moving on their own. It's just... I don't know, it's really hard to explain. Like I was saying, it's almost like a trance, but I am still the one opening the pantry door, you know? I'm the one reaching into the box of crackers. 

I guess what I mean is, I don't sit there and think, 'I am going to eat this entire sleeve of crackers and then move on to the cookies.' It just sort of happens. I'll be standing there in the dark, the refrigerator light humming—it has this very specific, low hum that seems so loud at 2:00 AM when the rest of the house is dead silent—and I'll just be eating. And maybe I could stop if I really, really tried, or if my husband walked in and startled me, but in the moment, I just... don't. I don't stop. 

So, I don't know if that means I've lost control, or if I'm just choosing not to exercise it because I'm so exhausted from everything else. Does that make sense? It's not a complete blackout, loss-of-my-faculties kind of thing. It's more like I'm just on autopilot, and the autopilot happens to be steering me toward the sweets. So, no, I wouldn't say I completely lose control, but I'm definitely not making mindful, conscious choices either. It's just a very strange, detached feeling.
Do you ever eat a large amount of food in a short period of time, like during those late-night episodes?

A large amount in a short time? Um... no, I wouldn't really say that. It’s not like I’m sitting down and just shoveling a whole cake or a massive meal into my mouth in five minutes. It’s definitely not like that. It’s much more of a slow... a slow grazing, I guess you could call it. 

Like, I’ll take a cracker. Just one. And I’ll stand there, usually leaning against the edge of the counter—and the kitchen tile gets so incredibly cold on my bare feet because I almost never remember to put my slippers on when I get out of bed at that hour—and I’ll just chew that one cracker while I look out the window over the sink at the streetlights. And then maybe five or ten minutes will go by, just listening to the house settle and watching the shadows, and then I’ll reach into the box for another one. Or maybe I’ll switch to the tin of cookies my mother-in-law brought over on Sunday. 

So, I might actually be down there in the dark for an hour, or even two hours sometimes. It’s definitely not a short period of time. It’s just this long, drawn-out stretch of being awake when the rest of the world is asleep. And over the course of those two hours, I mean, sure, I guess the crackers and the little sweets add up eventually, but it never feels like a massive amount of food all at once. It’s just a bite here, a bite there, while my mind is either completely blank or completely racing about silly things like whether I remembered to switch the laundry over to the dryer or what we're going to do about the gutters before it rains again. So, no, I wouldn't say it’s a huge amount really fast. It’s just a very slow, quiet nibbling that just kind of stretches on and on until my legs get tired of standing there.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?

Weight? Oh, well, you know, it's funny you ask that because, honestly, I don't really weigh myself that often. We have a scale in the bathroom, one of those digital ones that my husband bought a few years ago because he was trying to track his fitness, but I usually just kind of ignore it. But, even without stepping on the scale, I can definitely tell that things are shifting, mostly by the way my clothes fit. And like I was saying before—and I know I keep coming back to this, but it really is the whole reason I finally picked up the phone and made this appointment—my eating has just been completely all over the place. 

It's just so erratic, and I think my body doesn't know what to do with it. Because, like I mentioned, there are those weeks where I will make a beautiful dinner, like a roast chicken with vegetables, and I'll sit down at the table with my husband, and I just barely touch it. I just move the food around my plate, and my stomach feels completely tied in knots, or I just have zero interest in it whatsoever. So during those times, I'm sure I'm dropping a few pounds because I'm practically running on empty. My jeans definitely feel looser around the waist on those days. 

But then, the pendulum swings, and I have those nights where I'm standing in the kitchen at two in the morning, after everyone else has gone to bed, and I'm just eating crackers and sweets in the dark for an hour or two. And all those little empty calories from the cookies and the snacking, well, they definitely catch up with you. So then my clothes start feeling snug again, especially around my middle, which is incredibly frustrating when you're trying to get dressed in the morning and nothing feels quite right. So, I wouldn't say I've gained or lost a massive amount of weight in one direction, but it's just this constant, exhausting yo-yo effect because my eating habits are just completely unpredictable right now.
Do you usually feel guilty after eating, aside from the late-night episodes?

Guilty? Um... no, not really. I mean, outside of those weird late-night things where I'm just standing there in the dark, I don't really feel guilty about eating during the day. Like, when I actually do eat a normal meal, which, as I was saying, is really hit or miss lately. But on the days where I do sit down and have lunch, say, a turkey sandwich or a salad, I don't sit there afterward and beat myself up about it. It's just food, you know? It's just fuel to get through the afternoon, to have enough energy to maybe run to the grocery store or fold that laundry I was worrying about the night before.

I don't have this constant running tally in my head about calories or feeling like I've committed some sort of crime by eating a piece of bread. It's really only when things get so completely out of whack, like when I'm just not eating at all for days because my stomach is in knots, or when I'm doing that slow, mindless grazing at 2:00 AM. That's when I feel... well, maybe not even guilty, just confused and frustrated with myself. Because I know it's not normal to stand barefoot on cold tile eating saltines for an hour. But during a regular Tuesday afternoon if I have a bowl of soup? No, no guilt at all. I just eat it, wash the bowl, put it in the drying rack—I always hand wash my soup bowls because they take up too much room in the dishwasher—and then I just go about my day. So, no, guilt isn't really a part of the everyday eating for me.
Do you think eating helps you cope with your feelings of guilt and anxiety?

Cope with guilt and anxiety? Um... no, I don't think so. Actually, it's really the complete opposite for me. 

Because, like I was saying just a minute ago, I don't really have that guilt around food itself. And as for the anxiety... well, when I'm feeling really anxious, you know, when my thoughts are just spinning out of control about everything and nothing all at once—like worrying if the car needs an oil change, or if I said the wrong thing to my sister on the phone last Tuesday, or just this heavy, general sense of dread that I can't even put my finger on—eating is the absolute last thing on my mind. 

People always talk about "comfort eating," don't they? Like in the movies where someone has a terrible day and they just sit on the couch with a giant tub of chocolate ice cream and a spoon, crying and eating. I have never, ever understood that. For me, anxiety feels like this physical block right in the middle of my throat, and my stomach just completely clenches up. If I try to force myself to eat when I'm feeling that wound up, it honestly feels like I'm trying to swallow dry sand. 

My husband, bless his heart, he tries to help. When he sees me pacing or getting really tense, he’ll try to make me a cup of chamomile tea or he'll bring me a piece of dry toast because he thinks having something in my stomach will settle my nerves. But I just end up staring at it on the coffee table until the tea goes completely cold and the toast gets stale. I just can't do it. So, no, food doesn't soothe me or help me cope with those feelings at all. If anything, when the anxiety is really bad, food just becomes this exhausting chore that I completely avoid because my stomach is already doing flip-flops. It definitely doesn't make me feel any better.
Has your erratic eating pattern affected your relationships with family and friends?

Affected my relationships? Um... no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say it's caused any actual problems or fights or anything like that. 

Because, well, my husband—like I was saying earlier about him trying to bring me toast and tea—he’s just incredibly patient with the whole thing. He doesn't get angry when I don't eat the dinner he helped chop vegetables for, or when he finds the empty cracker sleeves in the recycling bin the next morning. He just... he worries, I think, but it doesn't put a wedge between us or make him resent me. 

And as for my friends or the rest of my family, like my sister... well, I don't really eat in front of them all that much anyway right now. We used to do this monthly brunch thing, a few of the girls from my old neighborhood, at this little cafe downtown that makes these huge, wonderful blueberry scones. I used to look forward to it so much. But, you know, since I haven't been working and everyone's schedules just got so incredibly busy with their kids and their own lives, we haven't actually done that in months. We just sort of drifted out of the habit. So they aren't even really around to see me being weird with food. 

If I talk to my sister on the phone—we usually talk on Tuesday afternoons because she has a long drive back from her mother-in-law's house and needs someone to keep her awake—I might mention that my stomach is off or that I haven't been eating right, but she just listens. She doesn't judge me or get frustrated. She's always been the easygoing one in the family anyway. So, no, I don't think my eating habits have ruined any friendships or caused any real issues with my family at all. It's mostly just something I'm dealing with in my own house, mostly in my own head, you know? Nobody is pulling away from me just because my appetite is a mess.
Are there any activities or tasks that you've had to stop doing or avoid because of your eating habits?

Stop doing things? Um... no, not because of the eating, anyway. 

Since I'm not working right now—which I think I mentioned—my days are pretty open, so I still do all the normal stuff around the house. The eating habits haven't gotten in the way of that. Like the laundry, for example. Even if I haven't eaten anything but those saltines the night before and my stomach feels completely hollow, I still manage to get the clothes sorted and washed. I'm very particular about sorting, actually—whites, darks, and then a totally separate load just for towels, because I absolutely hate when towel lint gets on my husband's work slacks. He wears these navy blue pants that just attract every single speck of dust, and if I wash them with the towels, I end up spending twenty minutes with a lint roller. So I still do all of that.

And grocery shopping... I still go to the store, too. It's actually kind of a funny experience, going to the grocery store when your stomach is in knots and you have absolutely no appetite. You're walking down the aisles looking at all this food—the bright produce section, the bakery smelling like fresh bread—and it all just seems so completely irrelevant to you. Like you're shopping for a stranger. But I still go, I still push the cart with the wonky wheel, I still buy the chamomile tea and the bread for the toast my husband tries to make me, and all the vegetables he likes to chop for dinner. I just don't always eat it. 

So, no, the eating itself, or the not eating, hasn't forced me to cancel plans or avoid my daily chores. I mean, I might do things a little slower if my energy is low because I skipped lunch, like taking my time folding those towels or maybe sitting down at the kitchen island while I sort the mail instead of standing up, but I don't avoid the tasks completely. I just push through it, you know? Because the house still needs to run, even if my appetite is completely out to lunch... pun intended, I guess. But yeah, no, I haven't had to stop doing anything at all.
Are you finding it harder to concentrate on your daily tasks due to your eating habits?

Concentrate? Um, no... no, I wouldn't say the eating thing affects my concentration at all. It's actually kind of surprising, isn't it? You'd think if you're running on empty, your brain would just sort of turn to mush, but... well, for me, it really doesn't. 

Like, just yesterday morning, I sat down at the kitchen island to go through the mail and balance the checkbook. I still do it by hand, by the way, because I just don't trust all these online banking apps. My husband is always telling me it's perfectly safe and that I'm making extra work for myself, but I just really like seeing the numbers written out in my own handwriting, usually in blue ink, right there in the ledger. It makes me feel organized. Anyway, I hadn't eaten anything but a few sips of that cold chamomile tea from the night before, and my stomach was completely hollow, but I was still able to focus perfectly fine. I went through every single receipt from the grocery store—the one with the wonky cart wheel I was telling you about—checked off the utility bills, and did all the math without a single mistake. I sat there for a good hour, totally zeroed in on what I was doing. 

So, my mind is still sharp when it comes to the tasks I need to get done. If I get distracted or lose my train of thought, it's usually just because my mind is already racing about other things, you know, that heavy anxiety I mentioned earlier where I'm worrying about the car or my sister. But it's definitely not because I skipped breakfast or didn't eat enough dinner. The food—or the lack of food, I should say—doesn't make me foggy or mess with my attention span in the slightest. I can still focus just fine, even if my stomach is completely empty.
Do you worry about gaining weight when you're eating normally or during these late-night episodes?

Weight? Oh, um... no. No, I really don't. 

I mean, I know a lot of women my age—I'm 46, you know—start really obsessing over their metabolism slowing down and every little pound they put on. My sister is always talking about her latest diet, keto this and paleo that, and how she can't even look at a carbohydrate without going up a dress size. But for me? No. I've actually been pretty much the exact same size since my late twenties. 

And even with those late-night episodes... I mean, how much weight can you really gain from half a sleeve of unsalted saltines, anyway? It's not like I'm sneaking down to the kitchen and eating an entire chocolate cake or making myself a four-course meal at two in the morning. It's just dry crackers. And honestly, my husband has always said he wouldn't care if I gained a few pounds anyway. He's so sweet about it. I have this one pair of jeans, these dark wash bootcut ones that I bought at a department store clearance sale maybe five or six years ago, and they still fit exactly the same as the day I bought them. If they ever get a little snug, it's usually just because I accidentally dried them on high heat instead of tumbling them on low, not because I've actually put on weight. 

So, no, when my stomach is actually letting me eat normally, or when I'm just sitting in the dark at the kitchen island with my tea and my crackers, the number on the scale is the absolute furthest thing from my mind. I'm just trying to get something, anything, to settle in my stomach so I can go back to sleep. Gaining weight just isn't something that crosses my radar at all.
Do you ever worry that your eating habits might cause you to gain weight?

Weight? Oh, well... I think I just mentioned this, actually. No, I really don't worry about gaining weight. 

I mean, like I said, I've been pretty much the same size for years. My sister is the one always agonizing over the scale, trying to cut out bread or dairy or whatever the new fad is. But for me, it's just never been a concern. Especially lately, because, I mean, the way I've been eating—or not eating—it's really just about trying to get my stomach to settle down. Like I was saying about the saltines at two in the morning. You can't really pack on the pounds with a few dry crackers and some chamomile tea, you know? 

And honestly, when I am able to eat normally, I'm just so relieved that I can actually get through a meal without feeling completely nauseated or hollowed out. The thought of, "Oh, is this going to make me gain a pound?" just doesn't even enter my brain. I'm just focused on getting the nutrition in and hoping it stays down and doesn't make my stomach churn. So, no, the weight thing... it's just really not on my radar at all. I'm much more concerned with just trying to feel normal again, you know? Like, just being able to sit down at the dinner table with my husband and eat the vegetables he chopped without feeling like it's a chore. That's what I worry about, not the number on the scale.
Do you think your eating habits are related to a fear of gaining weight?

Wait, didn't I... I feel like we just covered this, didn't we? I'm sorry if I wasn't being clear before, but no, absolutely not. It has zero to do with being afraid of gaining weight. Like I was just saying a minute ago, my weight is really the absolute last thing on my mind. 

I mean, if I was actually afraid of gaining weight, I'd probably be acting like my sister, right? She has this little digital food scale on her kitchen counter—it's glass and stainless steel, very modern looking, she got it on Amazon—and she literally weighs every single almond or piece of cheese she puts in her mouth. It is honestly exhausting just watching her do it. But me? I don't even know where our bathroom scale is. I think it got shoved under the guest bathroom sink behind some extra rolls of toilet paper and a bottle of bleach maybe three or four years ago when we were repainting the baseboards in there, and I haven't even thought to look for it since. 

So, no, when I'm sitting there at two in the morning eating saltines—and I only buy the name brand ones, by the way, because the store brand always tastes a little like cardboard and they get stale so much faster—it's purely because my stomach is just in absolute knots. It's that awful, hollow, churning feeling I was telling you about, not some secret diet I'm on. I actually wish I could eat more, to be honest with you. I really wish I could just sit down and have a big plate of my husband's spaghetti and meatballs, with the garlic bread and everything, without feeling completely nauseous after two bites. The eating... or the not eating, I guess... it's just my body physically not letting me, or my mind racing too much about other things to just sit still for a proper meal. It is definitely, one hundred percent, not because I'm scared of going up a pants size.
Do you think your eating habits help you deal with emotional stress or difficult feelings?

Emotional stress? Hmm... I don't... I don't really think so. I mean, I know a lot of people do that, right? Emotional eating. Like you see it in movies all the time, someone goes through a bad breakup or has a terrible day at the office, and they come home and sit on the couch in their pajamas and eat an entire pint of Ben & Jerry's right out of the carton with a spoon. Usually Cherry Garcia or Chunky Monkey, right? And they just cry while they eat it. 

But for me, it doesn't really work like that. When I'm stressed out, or when my thoughts are just racing and racing and I can't get them to quiet down, or when I'm feeling really low and I can barely drag myself out of bed... food is the last thing I want. Like, my stomach just completely ties itself in these tight little knots, and the very idea of chewing and swallowing feels like climbing a mountain. I actually lose my appetite completely when I'm dealing with difficult feelings. 

And then, on the flip side, when I'm having one of those periods where my energy is just buzzing and I feel like I can do a million things at once—like last month when I decided I needed to reorganize the entire linen closet by color and thread count at three in the morning—I just forget to eat entirely. I'll be so focused on folding the towels perfectly so the edges line up exactly, and suddenly it's 4 PM the next day and I realize all I've had is three cups of coffee and a handful of dry cereal. 

So, no, I wouldn't say my eating habits help me deal with stress at all. If anything, the stress and the emotions completely dictate whether I can eat or not. It's more of a side effect, I guess? Like, the food isn't a comfort mechanism for me. It's just... either my body will let me have it, or it won't, depending on what's going on in my head. And like I said with the saltines, half the time I'm only eating those because my stomach is churning so badly from the anxiety or the stress that I just need something bland to soak up the acid so I don't feel like I'm going to be sick. It's not about feeling better emotionally, it's just about trying to stop the physical nausea.
Do you think eating helps you feel better when you're upset or anxious?

Wait, didn't we just... I mean, I feel like I literally just answered this, didn't I? About the emotional eating and the stress? 

But, I mean, no. To answer you again, no, eating does not help me feel better when I'm upset or anxious. It really doesn't. Like I was just saying about the ice cream thing, that whole cliché of eating your feelings? That's just not how my body works. When I'm anxious, when that really awful, tight feeling starts creeping up into my chest and my throat feels like it's closing over... the absolute last thing on this earth I want to do is try to force food down. 

I remember this one time, maybe a few months ago, my husband and I had this huge argument about... I don't even remember what it was about now, maybe the electric bill or something silly like that, but I was so worked up. My heart was just pounding, and my hands were shaking, and I felt like I couldn't catch my breath. And he had just made this beautiful roast chicken for dinner, with the little potatoes roasted underneath it so they soak up all the juices, with the rosemary and the garlic—he really is a wonderful cook, he watches all those cooking shows on PBS on Saturday afternoons and takes notes in this little spiral-bound notebook he keeps in the kitchen drawer next to the oven mitts. Anyway, he set this gorgeous plate of food down in front of me, and it smelled amazing, but I just looked at it and I started crying because my stomach was in such knots that I knew if I took even one bite, I would throw it right back up. 

So, no, eating doesn't soothe me. It doesn't calm me down. When I'm anxious, my stomach is just a rock. The only thing I can maybe handle is those saltines I keep talking about, and even then, I'm only eating them because the anxiety makes my stomach produce so much acid that I feel sick, and the crackers just kind of act like a sponge. It's purely mechanical, you know? It's not comforting at all. It's just survival mode until the anxiety passes or until my mind stops racing enough for me to actually realize I'm hungry. So, yeah, I definitely don't eat to feel better. I wish I could, sometimes, but I just can't.
Are there any situations or activities where you feel like your eating habits are impacting your ability to participate or enjoy them?

Honestly, it's not really the eating itself that's getting in the way of things, if that's what you're asking. Like, the saltines aren't stopping me from living my life. It's more... well, it's everything else that goes along with it, the whole state of mind I'm in. 

Because of all this, I’ve actually fallen really, really far behind on my facilitator training. I don't know if I mentioned that before, but I've been doing this training program, and usually I'm so on top of it. I have these color-coded binders for all the different modules, with the little plastic tabs so I can flip right to the section I need. But lately, my projects and all the explanations I have to write out for the assignments... they've just become so incredibly hard to organize. I sit down at my desk—I have this nice little oak desk in the corner of the living room by the window where the light is good—and I just stare at the screen. My thoughts get all tangled up, and I just can't figure out how to structure anything so it makes sense to anyone but me. 

And it's the exact same story with my private blog work. I have this little blog, mostly just a personal project for myself and a few friends, where I write things down, and I used to be so consistent with it. I'd update it every Tuesday and Friday morning without fail, usually with a cup of chamomile tea. But now? I just can't seem to put a coherent post together because I just can't organize my ideas. 

Plus, like I was saying earlier about that dinner with the roast chicken, the tension at home has just made it so much harder to keep up with any of our normal routines with my husband. We used to have such a nice, predictable rhythm to our days, you know? He'd cook, we'd sit down together at the table, we'd talk about our day. But now, with my stomach in knots and my head all over the place, that whole routine is completely out the window. So it's not the eating habits specifically that are the root of the problem, it's just that the tension and the mental disorganization are making it completely impossible to keep up with my training, my writing, or even just having a normal, quiet evening at home with my husband.
Do you think your eating habits are a way to cope with difficult emotions?

Okay, doctor, are you sure you're writing this down? Because I really feel like we are going in circles here. I know I talk a lot, and maybe my thoughts get a little jumbled, but I feel like I've answered this exact question three times now. 

But okay, let me try to explain it a different way, because maybe I'm just not being clear. It's not a coping mechanism. I'm not eating to soothe my feelings. Honestly, what finally pushed me to actually make this appointment and come in to see you is that my eating has just been completely all over the place. It’s entirely unpredictable. 

Like I was saying about that beautiful roast chicken my husband made... there are some weeks where I barely touch dinner. I will literally sit there at the dining room table—we have this lovely mahogany table that belonged to my grandmother, we always use placemats so we don't scratch the finish—and I'll just push a single green bean around my plate for forty-five minutes. My stomach is just a tight fist, and I can't eat a thing. 

But then, it's like my body gets confused, because there are other nights where I do the exact opposite. I'll wait until my husband is completely fast asleep. He's a very heavy sleeper, usually snoring softly on his left side, and the house gets so, so quiet. The floorboards in our hallway creak right near the bathroom, so I have to walk on the very outside edges of my feet just to get to the kitchen without waking him up.
